title: Soil physics

definition.text: The study of the physical properties and processes of soil, covering its solid, liquid and gas phases.

facts.text: It draws on physics, physical chemistry, engineering and meteorology and applies them to practical problems in agriculture, ecology and engineering.
Its results are used for management and prediction in both natural and managed ecosystems.
The soil physical processes that shape crop response to drainage include aeration, structure, stability and temperature.
Franklin Hiram King has been called the father of soil physics in the United States; he studied water-holding capacity, aeration and the movement of water in soils.
Edgar Buckingham (1867–1940) worked out the theory of gas diffusion in soil and of water flow in the vadose zone.
Willard Gardner was the first to measure capillary potential with porous cups and manometers, and predicted the moisture distribution above a water table.
Lorenzo A. Richards described water transport in unsaturated soil and measured soil water potential with a tensiometer.
John R. Philip found an analytical solution for soil water transport, and Martinus van Genuchten developed water retention and hydraulic conductivity functions.

notes: The 'Prominent soil physicists' list is folded into facts here; Buckingham, Gardner, Philip and van Genuchten are not founders, so they get no entries of their own.

definition.text: The mass of a soil or other particulate material divided by the whole volume it occupies, including the spaces between and within its particles.

facts.text: Unlike particle density, which excludes voids, bulk density depends on packing and changes with handling: a disturbed powder settles to a higher value.
In soil it depends mainly on the mineral make-up and the degree of compaction.
Quartz has a density of about 2.65 g/cm3, but the dry bulk density of a mineral soil is normally about half that, between 1.0 and 1.6 g/cm3.
Soils rich in organic carbon and some friable clays fall below 1.0 g/cm3, and peat soils range from 0.02 to 0.98 g/cm3.
Dry bulk density is inversely related to porosity: the more pore space a soil has, the lower its bulk density.
Measured at a standard moisture content, bulk density estimates compaction; a European Union study of the top 0-20 cm found croplands almost 1.5 times denser than woodlands.
A high value points either to compaction or to a mix of textures in which small particles fill the voids between coarse ones.
Humus lowers bulk density, and pedotransfer functions combine bulk density with particle size to estimate properties such as hydraulic conductivity.

conflicts.text: Most soils have a dry bulk density between 1.1 and 1.6 g/cm3.
conflicts.note: The Soil article gives 1.1 as the lower bound of the typical range; Bulk density (S:b0ea2daf5037) and Pore space in soil (S:886e31685869) give 1.0.

definition.text: Finding a soil's bulk density from an undisturbed core of known volume, weighed moist and again after oven drying.

facts.text: A metal corer is driven into the soil at the chosen depth and horizon, giving a sample of known total volume.
Weighing the moist core gives the wet, or total, bulk density; drying it in an oven, often at 105 °C until its weight is constant, gives the mass of solids.
The difference between the moist and dry masses is the material lost on drying, mostly water.
Dry bulk density is the oven-dry mass divided by the total volume; wet bulk density counts the liquids too.

title: Particle density

definition.text: The density of the solid particles of a soil or other material alone, not counting the voids between them.

facts.text: Soil particle density is typically 2.60 to 2.75 g/cm3 and usually stays the same for a given soil.
It is lower in soils high in organic matter and higher in soils rich in iron oxides.
Because bulk density includes the pores, it is always less than particle density, and unlike particle density it varies widely with biological activity and management.
Porosity can be calculated from bulk and particle density; a mean particle density of about 2.65 g/cm3 is used for silica sediments and 2.70 g/cm3 for carbonate ones.
Unlike bulk density, which depends on how loosely or tightly the material is packed, particle density is fairly well defined, though definitions differ on whether internal pores count.
With a pycnometer, the sample's volume is the pycnometer's volume minus the volume of a non-dissolving liquid of known density added to fill it.
A gas pycnometer finds the sample volume from the pressure change when gas from a reservoir expands into the sample chamber, using Boyle's law.
Buoyancy methods include weighing the sample in air and in a liquid, a hydrometer in a slurry, or a density-gradient column where particles settle at their own density.

conflicts.text: Soil particle density is in the range of 2.6 to 2.7 g/cm3.
conflicts.note: Typical range from the Soil article; Physical properties of soil (S:9490520a201c) gives an upper bound of 2.75 g/cm3.

notes: Article now crawled (Particle mass density); the soil-specific values come from Physical properties of soil, Bulk density, Porosity and Soil.

definition.text: The share of a material's total volume taken up by empty spaces, given as a fraction from 0 to 1 or as a percentage.

facts.text: In geology, hydrology and soil science it describes the void fraction of a porous medium such as rock or sediment, whose voids may hold air or water.
Written ϕ or n, it ranges from less than 0.005 in solid granite to more than 0.5 in peat and clay.
It can be calculated from bulk density and particle density; when the voids hold air, porosity is one minus bulk density divided by particle density.
Well-sorted materials are more porous than poorly sorted ones of similar size, in which small particles fill the gaps between larger ones.
A few fine grains lodged in the pores can sharply cut porosity and hydraulic conductivity while making up only a small share of the volume.
The porosity of a rock or sedimentary layer governs how much water or hydrocarbon it may hold.
Sediment porosity falls exponentially with burial depth as it compacts, a relationship described by the Athy (1930) equation.

definition.text: The pattern by which surface-soil porosity falls as particle size rises, because fine-textured soils build aggregates.

facts.text: Sandy soil, typically 1.5 to 1.7 g/cm3 in bulk density, has a porosity between 0.43 and 0.36; clay soil at 1.1 to 1.3 g/cm3 has between 0.58 and 0.51.
Calling clay soils heavy seems to imply low porosity; the word reflects their moisture weight and the extra force needed to pull tillage tools through them.
Subsurface soil is less porous than surface soil because gravity compacts it; 0.20 is normal for unsorted gravel-sized material below the biomantle.
Traditional models treat soil porosity as continuous and give only approximate results, so fractal, cracking, packed-sphere and other models have been proposed.

definition.text: The loose link between how much pore space a material has and how easily water flows through it.

facts.text: Of two similar sandy aquifers, the more porous one usually conducts water faster, but the proportionality is inferred rather than direct.
Conductivity tracks pore-throat radius closely; as grain size or sorting decreases, the tie between throat radius and porosity, and so conductivity, breaks down.
Clays have very high porosity but very low conductivity: they store much water per volume but release it slowly through narrow pore throats.

definition.text: Categories that distinguish pore systems by their origin and by whether fluids can flow through them, such as primary, secondary, effective and dual porosity.

facts.text: Primary porosity is the original pore system of a rock or alluvial deposit; secondary porosity forms later, through leaching of minerals or fracturing.
Effective, or open, porosity is the fraction where fluid actually flows, excluding closed pores; it matters for groundwater flow and solute transport.
Ineffective, or closed, porosity holds fluids or gases that cannot flow.
Dual porosity treats a medium as two overlapping reservoirs that interact, such as the rock mass and its fractures.

title: IUPAC pore size classification

definition.text: A standard division of pores, set by IUPAC in 1985, into micropores under 2 nm, mesopores of 2 to 50 nm and macropores over 50 nm across.

facts.text: The limits come from how gases adsorb on rigid solids: micropores fill cooperatively, mesopores show capillary condensation, and in macropores confinement effects vanish.
The scheme grew out of earlier frameworks by M. M. Dubinin and D. H. Everett.
Outside chemistry the IUPAC limits are often ignored and the prefixes only mark relative pore sizes, which causes confusion between disciplines.

notes: Materials-science scale. Soil pore classes (Brewer 1964, Pore space in soil#Pore types) use micrometre limits, so 'micropore' and 'macropore' mean different sizes in the two schemes; useful as a contrast.

definition.text: Laboratory and imaging techniques that find the pore volume of a sample, either directly or from the fluid it takes up.

facts.text: Direct methods subtract the volume of the solid skeleton from the bulk volume; optical methods compare pore and solid areas under a microscope.
Water saturation and water evaporation methods find pore volume from the water a soaked sample holds, comparing its saturated and dry weights.
The gas expansion method lets gas pass from the sample's container into an evacuated one and applies the ideal gas law; it detects only pores open to the surroundings.
Computed tomography renders voids in three dimensions, while mercury intrusion and thermoporosimetry give information on pore sizes.

definition.text: The part of a soil's volume not filled by its solid mineral and organic particles, which holds the soil's water and air.

facts.text: Total porosity is the pore volume divided by the total volume, often given in percent; in unsaturated soil the pores are shared by air and water.
Porosity depends on the soil's minerals and on sorting: a sandy soil is more porous than a silty sand, because silt fills the gaps between sand grains.
Pure sand resists compaction and raises porosity, but not when mixed with finer minerals that fill the voids between its grains.
Macropores and cracks largely control infiltration rates, preferential flow, hydraulic conductivity and evapotranspiration, and strongly affect gas exchange and soil respiration.
When water infiltrates, the largest cracks and pores fill first, mostly by gravity; smaller pores fill slowly by capillary forces and can trap air.
Hydraulic conductivity, the ease of water movement through pores, depends on permeability, compaction and degree of saturation and is calculated with Darcy's law.
Pore space is the habitat of roots, soil fauna and microbes, and growing roots and burrowing animals create networks of connected pores.
Microbial cells and the slime they produce can block soil pores, a process called bioclogging.

definition.text: A widely used grouping of soil pores by diameter, after Brewer (1964), from macropores down to cryptopores, each class playing a different part for water and life.

facts.text: Macropores, over 75 μm, are too large for significant capillary force; unless closed off they drain and are usually air-filled at field capacity.
Macropores form by cracking, by separation of peds and aggregates, and through roots and burrowing animals.
Mesopores, 30–75 μm, are the largest pores still water-filled at field capacity; called storage pores, they hold water that plants and soil organisms can use.
Micropores, 5–30 μm, hold water that is practically immobile yet still available to plants, so solutes move through them mainly by diffusion.
Ultramicropores, 0.1–5 μm, shelter microbes inside aggregates from predators such as amoebae and nematodes; their volume correlates with bacterial biomass.
Ultramicropores are set by texture and organic matter and are little affected by compaction.
Cryptopores, under 0.1 μm, are too small for most microbes, so organic matter inside them is protected from decay; their water is barely available to plants.
Soil scientists study mesopores closely because of their importance for agriculture and irrigation.

definition.text: Ways of measuring and simulating cracks in soil, which shape infiltration, gas exchange and the effects of compaction.

facts.text: Early field methods traced crack patterns by hand or measured cracks inside a wire semicircle moved along a string line, estimating their distribution with Buffon's needle.
Horgan and Young (2000) built a two-dimensional computer model of surface crack growth, based on cracks attracting one another once they come close.
The model could not predict where cracking starts; soil cracking is often not random but follows lines of weakness.
Because air has infinite resistivity, electrical resistivity imaging can map the air-filled cracks in a soil.

definition.text: A way of imaging soil pores by filling an undisturbed core with fluorescent resin, then grinding and photographing it layer by layer.

facts.text: A representative undisturbed core is impregnated with low-viscosity synthetic resin mixed with a fluorescent dye such as fluorescein.
The core is ground back about 1 mm per step, and each new face is lit with ultraviolet or blue light and photographed with a digital camera.
Computer image analysis then measures depth, continuity, surface area and other properties of the resin-filled cracks.

definition.text: The ratio of the volume of voids, filled with gas or liquid, to the volume of solids in a soil or other porous material.

facts.text: It is a dimensionless number closely tied to porosity, which instead divides the void volume by the total volume.
The simple relation assumes a rigid skeleton whose volume does not change on wetting or drying, so swelling clays such as smectite, with water bound between their layers, fall outside it.
Geotechnical engineering treats void ratio, symbol e, as a state variable of soils; because ϕ there denotes the angle of shearing resistance, porosity is written η.
A loose soil with a high void ratio tends to shrink under load as voids close and grain contacts increase, which changes its effective stress.
A dense soil with a low void ratio tends to swell when unloaded, and partly dry smectite clay particles swell as they take up water.
Loose soils conduct water readily while dense ones are less permeable; fine particles pass through the large voids of loose soil but clog the small pores of dense soil.
For a given soil, the coefficient of permeability rises with the void ratio.

definition.text: The state of a soil whose water content is below its porosity, so that its pores hold air as well as water.

facts.text: In saturated aquifers every pore is water-filled, so volumetric water content equals porosity; the capillary fringe above the water table divides saturated from unsaturated conditions.
Unsaturated soils are the subject of vadose zone hydrogeology; water content in the capillary fringe falls with height above the water table.
As a soil dries its connected wet pathways shrink, so unsaturated hydraulic conductivity falls with water content in a strongly non-linear way.
Water moving through unsaturated soil often advances in fingers, caused by Saffman–Taylor instability at an unstable boundary between wet and dry zones.

title: Aggregate moisture conditions

definition.text: The four moisture states used for construction aggregates: oven-dry, air-dry, saturated surface dry and damp.

facts.text: Oven-dry aggregate holds no moisture and is reached by heating to 105 °C; air-dry aggregate has moisture in its pores but dry outer surfaces.

Saturated surface dry aggregate has water-filled voids but surfaces that neither absorb nor give up mixing water; it is the usual starting condition for laboratory tests on materials such as concrete.

notes: Construction-materials (concrete aggregate) testing, not soil science; drafted only because it is its own section of a seed page.

definition.text: The densification of soil under applied stress as air is pushed out of the pores between its grains.

facts.text: When water rather than air is squeezed out, the process is consolidation; in soil science and agronomy compaction usually mixes the two and can be driven by suction as water evaporates.
It is normally caused by heavy machinery, but the passage of animal feet can also compact soil.
Compacted soils absorb less rainfall, so runoff and erosion increase.
Pressed-together grains leave little space for the air and water roots need, and burrowing animals find the denser soil hard to penetrate.
In one cotton field, tilled surface soil had a bulk density of 1.3 g/cm3 and 51% pore space, while wheel-trafficked inter-rows had 1.67 g/cm3 and 37%.
Recovery depends on climate, mineralogy and fauna; high shrink–swell soils such as Vertisols recover quickly where dry spells shrink and crack them.
Kaolinite clays, which do not crack as they dry, cannot recover unaided unless earthworms or other ground-dwelling animals live in them, as in the Cecil soil series.
Soil compaction is one of the factors that reduce groundwater recharge.

title: Compaction in construction

definition.text: Deliberately densifying soil with heavy equipment so that it can support foundations, roads, walkways and retaining structures.

facts.text: Fill soil should be strong, relatively incompressible, stable against volume change as water content varies, durable and suitably permeable; it is placed in layers called lifts.
Grain-size distribution, grain shape, specific gravity of the solids and the amount and type of clay minerals strongly influence the maximum dry unit weight and optimum moisture content.
Sands and gravels are usually compacted with vibrating equipment, while silts and clays are often worked with a sheepsfoot roller, whose intense local shearing drives out air.
After construction, areas to be landscaped need to be decompacted so that vegetation can grow.

notes: Engineering practice; kept (not excluded) as the counterpart to agricultural compaction and for the decompaction point. The procedural detail sits in the two excluded entries below.

title: Engineering compaction methods

definition.text: The ways stress is applied to compact soil and other materials in construction: static, impact, vibrating, gyrating, rolling and kneading.

facts.text: Methods that apply significant shear as well as compressive stress are generally the most effective.
Static loading applies a large stress slowly, impact drops a large mass, and vibration applies rapid repeated stress through a plate or hammer.
Rolling passes a heavy cylinder over the surface, often with vibration; kneading alternates shear in adjacent positions, as the sheepsfoot roller does at landfills.

notes: Pure geotechnical/construction procedure, outside a soil science course.

title: Laboratory compaction tests

definition.text: Laboratory tests that relate a soil's moulding water content to its dry unit weight, to set compaction targets for engineering fill.

facts.text: Adequate field compaction is judged by comparing in-situ density with the maximum density from a laboratory test, most commonly the Proctor test.
There are standard and modified Proctor tests; the modified one is more common, though the standard test may still be the reference for small dams.
The maximum dry density and optimum moisture content, found before field work, set the density to be reached in the field.
Greater compaction strengthens fine-grained and gypsiferous soils by lowering void ratio and raising dry density, which improves particle interlocking.

notes: Geotechnical test procedure (Proctor; ASTM D698, D1557 and similar standards), not core soil science.

title: Soil compaction in agriculture

definition.text: The rise in bulk density, or fall in porosity, of farmland soil under externally or internally applied loads, also called soil structure degradation.

facts.text: It can harm nearly all physical, chemical and biological properties and functions of soil, and with erosion it is called the costliest and most serious environmental problem of conventional agriculture.
Heavy machinery and poor management can compact the subsoil, forming impermeable layers that restrict water and nutrient cycles.
Unlike salinization or erosion it is mainly a hidden, sub-surface problem, so special identification methods are needed to locate and manage it.
On site it cuts crop growth, yield and quality; off site it adds runoff, erosion, greenhouse gas emissions, eutrophication, reduced groundwater recharge and biodiversity loss.
Plough-pans were linked to compaction before farming was mechanized, but modern farming techniques have raised the risk of harmful compaction.
In 1991 compaction was estimated to account for 4% (68.3 million hectares) of human-caused soil degradation worldwide.
In 2013 it was a major cause of degradation in Europe (about 33 million ha), Africa (18 million ha), Asia (10 million ha) and Australia (4 million ha).
In Europe about 32% of subsoils are highly and 18% moderately vulnerable to compaction.

notes: Soil compaction (the engineering-framed page, part02) and this page describe overlapping things; kept as two entries because the sources treat construction compaction and farmland compaction separately. Merge if selection prefers one.

definition.text: How pressure on soil is taken up by closer particle contacts, shrinking the voids and squeezing out water and air, and which soil properties make that easier or harder.

facts.text: In well-structured soil, particles bond into aggregates whose stability grows with the number of particle interactions; water films around particles can shield those interactions and weaken structure.
Applied pressure is countered by more particle contacts, which shrinks the voids, displaces water and air, raises bulk density and lowers permeability to water and air.
Fine-textured, clay-rich soils are more susceptible than coarse ones, and wet soils more than dry ones, because water films shield particle contacts.
Angular, heterogeneous structure, a high initial bulk density and organic matter, which binds minerals and water, all raise resistance to compaction.
Soil pH also matters, because it affects the net charges of molecules.

definition.text: The natural and human drivers of compaction on farmland, chiefly heavy machinery, tillage and livestock trampling.

facts.text: Compaction can occur naturally through drying and wetting, called consolidation, or when external pressure is applied.
Heavy machinery compacts the subsoil as well as the topsoil, and subsoil compaction is harder to reverse.
Axle load, speed, number of passes and tyre inflation pressure all affect how severely machinery compacts soil.
Tillage itself can compact soil, though over the long term it may leave less topsoil compaction than no tillage; heavy livestock trampling, set by grazing intensity, is another major cause.

definition.text: The on-site and off-site consequences of compaction for soil air and water, plants, soil life, climate, water bodies and food supply.

facts.text: Compaction chiefly reduces air permeability and water infiltration.
Higher bulk density and smaller pores restrict roots, partly through build-up of the hormone ethylene, and limit nutrient access; shallow roots can leave the topsoil extremely dry and cracked.
Poorer oxygen diffusion can make soil anaerobic and, with wetter conditions, boosts denitrification, raising N2O emissions and lowering the nitrogen available to crops.
Severe compaction can reduce microbial biomass and, by removing large pores, change the distribution of earthworms and other macrofauna.
Waterlogged compacted soils release methane through increased bacterial activity, and poorer nitrogen use means more fuel and fertilizer per crop.
Wheel tracks on compacted soil often start runoff and erosion, carrying sediment, nutrients and pesticides beyond the field and feeding eutrophication of surface waters.
Grassland soil without traffic takes in water five times faster than severely trafficked soil, so compaction can reduce groundwater recharge, a serious risk in dry regions.
Added up over large areas, the yield losses may threaten food security, especially where droughts and floods are common, and climate change can worsen the effects.

definition.text: Field, laboratory and remote-sensing methods for detecting compacted soil, used in combination because no single method suffices.

facts.text: Field signs include waterlogging, visibly reduced porosity and changed structure, moisture and colour; poor aeration can give a blue-grey colour and a smell of hydrogen sulphide.
A penetrometer measures the rise in soil strength; crop growth patterns, pale leaves and root growth also reveal compaction, best judged against nearby uncompacted soil.
In the laboratory, bulk density, pore-size distribution, water permeability and gas diffusion show the degree of compaction, with attention on the coarse pores.
Remote sensing can map susceptibility from texture, slope, water regime and farming type but cannot detect compaction directly, which often varies within a few square metres.

title: Compaction avoidance and mitigation

definition.text: Biological, chemical and technical measures, backed by policy, that prevent soil compaction or help compacted soil recover.

facts.text: Partial restoration of compacted soil takes several decades, so avoiding and alleviating compaction is essential.
Deep-rooting crops regenerate compacted soil: their roots break impermeable layers and add organic matter, and they drive wetting and drying cycles that crack the soil.
Converting conventional farms to agroforestry, which grows crops and trees on the same site, regenerates compacted soil over the long run.
Zaï planting pits, 20–40 cm across and 10–20 cm deep, are filled with organic matter and seeded after the first rain; they capture water and gradually rehabilitate the soil beneath.
Liming raises pH and base saturation to suit microbes and earthworms, whose activity loosens the soil and improves porosity and permeability to water and air.
Controlled traffic keeps wheel tracks apart from rooting areas, and low tyre pressure spreads machinery loads over a larger surface.
Deep ripping can loosen layers that are already compacted, and modelling field vulnerability helps farmers avoid driving on susceptible soil.
The EU's Seventh Environment Action Programme, in force from 2014, addresses compaction, and Germany's Federal Soil Conservation Law obliges farmers to take precautions against it.

notes: The zaï sentence S:982fc981edcd carries a CITATION NEEDED tag; Zaï has its own crawled page owned elsewhere.

title: Soil mechanics

definition.text: The branch of soil physics and applied mechanics that describes how soils behave.

facts.text: Unlike fluid or solid mechanics, it deals with a mixed material of fluids, usually air and water, and particles such as clay, silt, sand and gravel, plus organic solids.
Together with rock mechanics it is the theoretical basis of geotechnical engineering and engineering geology.
It analyses deformation of, and fluid flow within, structures built on, made of or buried in soil, such as foundations, retaining walls, dams and pipelines.
Its principles are also used in agricultural, coastal and geophysical engineering and in hydrology.
Normal stresses are shared between pore fluid and particles, but neither gas nor liquid resists shear, so shear resistance comes from friction and interlocking of the particles.
Engineering classification tests use dried, sieved and remoulded samples, so they miss the effects of soil structure or fabric and of pore size and pore fluid distribution.

notes: Course is soil science: the hub's genesis, mineralogy, grain-size, USCS, Atterberg, seepage, consolidation, slope, bearing-capacity and lateral-pressure sections are owned by other entries or chapters (pilot, chunks 05-08), so no section entries were drafted for them here.

title: Soil mass–volume relations

definition.text: The set of quantities that describe the proportions of air, water and solids in a soil, by volume and by mass.

facts.text: The notation separates the volumes, masses and weights of air, water and solids, giving equations for how the three phases of soil interact; weight is mass times gravitational acceleration.
The specific gravity of the solids, Gs, is their density divided by that of pure water, 1 g/cm3.
Wet or bulk density is total mass over total volume, taking the mass of air as zero; dry density counts only the mass of the solids.
Buoyant density, the mixture's density minus that of water, is used for soil submerged under water.
Water content, w, is the mass of water over the mass of solids, found by weighing a sample before and after oven drying.
Void ratio e and porosity n are interchangeable: n equals e/(1 + e), and e equals n/(1 − n).
Degree of saturation S is the volume of water over the volume of voids; combining the definitions expresses bulk density through Gs, S, e or w and the density of water.

notes: A soil phase diagram (air/water/solids by volume and mass) would teach these relations at a glance.

title: Relative density

definition.text: A measure of how densely packed a sand or gravel is, comparing its void ratio with its loosest and densest possible states.

facts.text: It is calculated from the in-situ void ratio and the maximum and minimum void ratios, which correspond to very loose and very dense states.
A relative density of 100% means very dense sand or gravel; 0% means extremely loose, unstable soil.
It is used for cohesionless soils, with calculation methods set out in ASTM D4254-00(2016).
It is defined as DR = (emax − e)/(emax − emin) × 100%; together with effective stress it controls the mechanical behaviour of cohesionless soil.

notes: Geotechnical index rather than a soil-survey property; kept as a concept a soil scientist may meet with sands.

title: Capillary action in soil

definition.text: The rise of water above the water table into the small pores of a soil, held there by surface tension under negative pressure.

facts.text: Soil can be fully saturated for some distance above the water table; higher up it is still wet, but its water content falls with elevation.
The height of capillary saturation depends on pore size, from about a centimetre in coarse sand to tens of metres in silt or clay.
Still water above the water table is at negative pressure, which pulls particles together, so effective stress can be positive even at a free surface.
That is why a wet sand castle stands, held by friction at the particle contacts, and collapses once it is submerged.
Negative pore pressures are much stronger in clay than in sand and explain why clay soils shrink as they dry and swell when wetted, which can damage light structures and roads.

notes: Soil-mechanics view of capillarity; water-in-soil owns Capillary fringe, which may cover the same rise from the hydrology side.

title: Soil shear tests

definition.text: Laboratory and field tests that measure the strength and stiffness parameters of soil.

facts.text: Laboratory tests include the direct shear, triaxial, simple shear, fall cone and hand shear vane tests.
In the ground, strength and stiffness are characterized with the cone penetration test and the standard penetration test.

notes: Geotechnical test procedures, outside a soil science course.

title: Lightweight deflectometer

definition.text: A portable in-situ device for quickly estimating soil stiffness and deformation.

facts.text: It is especially suited to field checks of subgrades and unbound materials in road engineering.

notes: Road-engineering field test; drafted only because it is its own section of a seed page.

definition.text: The pressure of the groundwater held in the pores between the particles of a soil or rock.

facts.text: Below the water table it is measured with piezometers and is generally close to hydrostatic, rising linearly with depth where the water is not flowing.
The water table lies at the depth where the water pressure equals atmospheric pressure.
In the unsaturated, or vadose, zone it is set by capillarity and called tension, suction or matric pressure; tensiometers measure it through a porous ceramic cup in contact with the soil.
It is essential for finding the stress state of soil, because Terzaghi's effective stress is the total stress minus the pore water pressure.

Its components include hydrostatic pressure from the weight of overlying material, osmotic pressure from uneven ion concentrations, and adsorption pressure from water films that draw particles together.
ISO 11276:1995 sets out tensiometer methods for measuring it in unsaturated and saturated soil and defines it as the sum of matric and pneumatic pressures.
Excess pore water pressure can force blocks out at the base of river banks, and rising pore pressure on slopes helps burst the surface layer in frost boils.

title: Matric suction
article: Pore water pressure#Above the water table

definition.text: The negative pore water pressure of unsaturated soil above the water table, caused by surface tension in the pores and defined as pore air pressure minus pore water pressure.

facts.text: Above the water table effective stress is roughly equal to total stress, and in fact slightly greater, because the pore water pressure there is negative.
Heavy rain that raises infiltration lowers matric suction along the soil water characteristic curve, cutting the soil's shear strength and slope stability.
The height of capillary rise is inversely proportional to pore diameter, so sandy soils have much shallower capillary zones than clays and silts.
A tensiometer measures matric water potential, or soil moisture tension, in the vadose zone.

title: Effective stress

definition.text: The part of the total stress in a soil that is carried by the solid skeleton rather than by the pore water.

facts.text: It equals the total normal stress minus the pore water pressure, a relationship Karl von Terzaghi first proposed in 1925.
Effective stress governs both the strength and the volume change of porous media, from sand, silt and clay to rock and concrete.
Soil strength comes mainly from friction between particles, which is proportional to normal stress, so higher pore water pressure lowers strength.
Because pore water is nearly incompressible, saturated soil can only be packed closer if water is squeezed out of its pores.
On level ground the total vertical stress at a point is the weight of everything above it per unit area, so it grows with depth in proportion to the density of the overlying soil.
Water injected between grains pushes them apart and lowers effective stress, while withdrawal forces them together; quicksand and the sandcastle effect are the two extremes.
Effective stress is central to slope stability and to groundwater-related subsidence.
In 1962 Jennings and Burland showed that volume change and shear strength of partly saturated soils do not follow effective stress changes alone.

notes: Terzaghi's principle (assigned page, chunk 08) covers the same relation; merge if the other pass drafts it as a separate entry.

definition.text: The largest shear stress a soil can sustain before it fails.

facts.text: Shear resistance comes from friction and interlocking of particles, and sometimes from cementation or bonding at particle contacts.
Because friction dominates, shear resistance on a plane is roughly proportional to the effective normal stress, so the angle of internal friction is closely related to the angle of repose.
Strength depends on effective stress, drainage conditions, particle density, strain rate and strain direction.
Interlocking makes soil expand or contract as it shears; if it expands, density and strength drop, so a peak strength may be followed by a fall in shear stress.
The state in which shear stress and density stay constant while strain continues is called the critical state, steady state or residual strength.
If water cannot flow in or out, shearing is undrained: particle density cannot change, but pore pressure and effective stress do; real soils are partially drained.
Knowing the strength shows whether a slope will stand, whether a building or bridge may settle too far, and what pressures act on a retaining wall.
Tresca theory is used for undrained, constant-volume shearing and Mohr–Coulomb theory for drained conditions; critical state and steady state theories are two major accounts of soil shear.

title: Factors controlling shear strength
article: Shear strength (soil)#Factors controlling shear strength of soils

definition.text: The soil properties and conditions that govern a soil's stress–strain behaviour and so its shear strength: composition, initial state, structure and loading.

facts.text: Composition covers mineralogy, grain size and its distribution, particle shape, the type and amount of pore fluid, and the ions on grains and in the pore fluid.
Initial state is set by void ratio, effective normal stress and stress history, and described with terms such as loose, dense, overconsolidated, normally consolidated, contractive or dilative.

Structure, the packing of particles, includes layers, fissures, slickensides and cementation; cements such as recrystallized calcium carbonate, or carbonate precipitated by microbes, bond particle contacts.
Loading conditions include drained or undrained stress paths and the magnitude, rate and history of loading, static or cyclic.

notes: Also drawn from Soil mechanics#Other factors and #Structure, fabric, and chemistry, which repeat the same list.

title: Undrained shear strength

definition.text: The shear strength a soil shows when it is sheared faster than the pore water pressure generated by shearing can dissipate.

facts.text: Dilating pores draw water in under negative pressure and contracting pores push it out under positive pressure; when shearing outpaces this flow, it is undrained.
Examples are rapid loading of sands in an earthquake, failure of a clay slope during heavy rain, and most failures during construction.
Undrained strength may be lower or higher than drained strength, depending on whether the soil is contractive or dilative.
It is usually defined by Tresca theory as Su, and for a given overconsolidation ratio its ratio to the original consolidation stress is roughly constant.

notes: Also drawn from Soil mechanics#Drained and undrained shear.

title: Drained shear strength

definition.text: The shear strength of a soil when pore pressures generated by shearing can dissipate as it shears, or when the soil is dry.

facts.text: It is usually approximated by the Mohr–Coulomb equation, which Terzaghi combined with effective stress in 1942: strength equals c′ plus effective normal stress times tan ϕ′.
ϕ′ is the angle of internal friction, whose tangent is the friction coefficient; peak, critical state and residual friction angles can all be defined.
The cohesion intercept c′ often results from forcing a straight line through data that actually curve, so it depends on the stress range and is not a fundamental soil property.
The failure envelope curves because the dilatancy of closely packed particles depends on confining pressure.

notes: Also drawn from Soil mechanics#Failure criteria (Coulomb equation, c′ not fundamental).

title: Critical state theory

definition.text: A theory of soil shearing that identifies a distinct strength, the critical state, at which soil keeps shearing at constant volume.

facts.text: Developed by Roscoe, Schofield and Wroth (1958), it distinguishes peak, critical state (constant volume) and residual strengths.
Loose soil contracts as it shears and may show no peak above the critical state; dense soil must dilate once its grains interlock, giving a peak followed by strain softening.
Dilative soils loosen and contractive soils densify as they shear until both reach a critical void ratio; the critical state line roughly separates the two behaviours.
Residual strength, below the critical state, develops when plate-like clay particles align into slickensides; allophanic clays without plate-like minerals tend not to show it.

contested_note: Sources report that the critical state concept drew much criticism for failing to match test data, chiefly because it ignores particle structure.
notes: Contested basis: S:b7ebf09d2ab1, S:1ca51fdfaa58. Also drawn from Soil mechanics#Friction, interlocking and dilation.

title: Steady state soil mechanics
article: Shear strength (soil)#Steady state (dynamical systems based soil shear)

definition.text: A refinement of the critical state idea in which soil deforms continuously at constant volume, effective stress, shear stress and velocity, with a statistically steady grain structure.

facts.text: Steve J. Poulos formally defined the steady state, building on a hypothesis of Arthur Casagrande; the approach is informally called Harvard soil mechanics.
Unlike the critical state, the grains take up a steady-state structure, aligned in the direction of shear for elongated particles; strong alignment corresponds to the residual condition.
It applies to drained and undrained shearing and to any granular material, including sands, and its value depends slightly on strain rate.

Dynamical systems-based soil mechanics (DSSM) treats soil deformation as a Poisson process in which particles reach their final positions at random shear strains, and fits stress–strain curves closely.

contested_note: The sources insist the steady state is not the critical state and list 'common misconceptions', showing the two schools disagree over the concepts.
notes: Also drawn from Soil mechanics#Recent developments (DSSM). Both sections lean on Poulos and Joseph (2012, 2017); verification should check for single-school framing (S:2a398314abc4, S:2a3f32c467c4).

title: Cohesion (geology)

definition.text: The part of a soil's or rock's shear strength that does not depend on friction between particles.

facts.text: True cohesion in soils comes from electrostatic forces in stiff overconsolidated clays, cementing by Fe2O3, CaCO3 or NaCl, negative capillary pressure, undrained pore pressure response and plant roots.
Several sources are temporary: weathering can remove electrostatic bonds, wetting removes capillary suction, time dissipates pore pressure, and logging or fire removes root cohesion.
Cohesive strength is usually measured with Mohr–Coulomb theory, in which it is the shear strength at zero normal pressure on the failure surface.
Typical values run from 0 to 48 kPa for very soft clay through 192 to 384 kPa for stiff clay to 384 to 766 kPa for very stiff clay.
When soil loses cohesion it can slough off banks and slopes.

notes: Table check for verification: S:4b050dee9a41 gives very stiff clay as 384 to 766 kPa but 28 to 110 psi; 384 kPa is about 56 psi, so the psi lower bound looks wrong. S:0d730298016c gives a generic 'Clay 10 to 20 kPa' row alongside the consistency classes.

definition.text: Cohesion-like strength in remoulded soft clay that comes from pore water suction and friction rather than from chemical bonds between particles.

facts.text: During critical state flow, undrained cohesion results from effective stress and critical state friction, not from bonds between particles.
Clay particles and chemicals in soft soil mainly create a measurable pore water suction; remoulded, the soil flows as a ductile plastic material with constant apparent cohesion.
Critical state soil mechanics treats the bearing capacity of soft clay as that of a perfectly plastic material with undrained apparent cohesion.

title: Angle of repose

definition.text: The steepest angle, measured from the horizontal, at which a granular material can be piled without slumping.

facts.text: At that angle the face of a pile is on the verge of sliding; rough, interlocking sand grains pile more steeply than smooth, rounded ones, which have less friction between them.
A little water bridging the gaps between grains raises the angle and the soil's strength, but saturation acts as a lubricant and can set off mass wasting.
Typical values are 15° for wet excavated clay, 15–30° for water-filled sand and 25–30° for natural gravel with sand; wind-blown sand builds up to about 34 degrees before sliding.
Henri Gautier recognized this 'natural slope' of soils in 1717; where it is exceeded, mass wasting and rockfall follow, so retaining walls hold soil where ground levels must change more steeply.

notes: Measurement methods (tilting box, fixed funnel, revolving cylinder) and the hopper/silo design uses were left out as particulate-engineering detail; results differ by method (S:4104189c8a63, S:d03965c70578).

title: Soil consolidation

definition.text: The gradual change in a soil's volume in response to a change in pressure, as water is slowly squeezed out of or drawn into its pores.

facts.text: When saturated soil is loaded, the water, far stiffer in volume than the soil skeleton, first carries the load as excess pore water pressure; as it seeps away, the matrix takes the load and shrinks.
A spring in a water-filled container with a hole in its lid models the process: the water resists the load at first, then drains out while the spring, the soil skeleton, shortens and takes over.
Saturated clays consolidate very slowly because their hydraulic conductivity is extremely low; coarse-grained soils drain readily and undergo immediate settlement instead.
Clays settle under external loads, under their own weight or that of overlying soil, and when groundwater pumping raises the effective stress on them.
Its effects are most visible where a building sits on soft, poorly permeable soil such as marine clay, which can settle a great deal over many years.
In the narrow sense the term means this delayed, drainage-driven response; in the broad sense it covers any pressure-driven volume change, including compaction, subsidence, heave and swelling.
Karl von Terzaghi, the 'father of soil mechanics', defined it as any decrease in the water content of a saturated soil without the water being replaced by air.
Engineers quantify it with the oedometer test, loading a thin disc of soil in steps and recording its thickness over time to find the coefficient of consolidation and hydraulic conductivity.

notes: Soil mechanics#Consolidation: transient flow of water (chunk 03) covers the same process; the merge should keep one entry.

definition.text: The change in a soil's void ratio for each tenfold increase in effective stress, a measure of how compressible it is during consolidation.

facts.text: Most theories assume void ratio falls with the logarithm of effective stress; the slope of that line, plotted from oedometer test data, is the compression index.
It ranges from 0.19 to 0.28 for kaolinite, 0.50 to 1.10 for illite and 1.0 to 2.6 for montmorillonite, depending on the ions the clay holds.
The more compressible the clay, the more its compressibility depends on cation type and electrolyte concentration.
Unloaded, a consolidated soil rebounds and regains some lost volume; reloaded, it consolidates again along a recompression curve defined by the recompression index.

definition.text: The state of a soil whose load has been removed, so that it now carries less than the highest stress it has ever borne.

facts.text: Soils that were once covered by glaciers, or affected by land subsidence, are overconsolidated.
The highest stress a soil has carried is its preconsolidation stress; the overconsolidation ratio (OCR) divides that stress by the current one.
A soil now under its highest stress is normally consolidated, with an OCR of one; just after a new load, before excess pore water pressure dissipates, it is underconsolidated.
Below the preconsolidation stress, settlement is calculated with the recompression index; loading beyond it adds virgin compression governed by the compression index.

definition.text: The slow change in a soil's volume at constant effective stress, also called creep or secondary compression, seen mainly in soils rich in organic matter.

facts.text: It is told apart from primary consolidation, the volume change caused as excess pore water pressure dissipates.
Creep comes from the viscous behaviour of the clay–water system and the compression of organic matter, and it continues slowly after pore pressure has returned to hydrostatic.
Most sands and clays low in organic matter show little creep, but peat creeps markedly and its poor consolidation makes it an unstable foundation for roads and buildings.
Its rate is assumed to decay exponentially with the time since loading, scaled by a secondary compression index.

title: Origins of consolidation theory

definition.text: The first modern theories of soil consolidation, proposed in the 1920s by Karl Terzaghi and Paul Fillunger along two very different lines.

facts.text: Terzaghi's simplified model, built on the diffusion equation, became engineering practice; Fillunger's rigorous mixture-theory model was too abstract to apply to real cases.
A bitter dispute between the two ended tragically in 1937 with Fillunger's suicide, after which his results were forgotten for decades.
Maurice Biot later developed the full three-dimensional theory, introducing the basic equations of poroelasticity.
Terzaghi's one-dimensional model is still the most used, because it is simple and rests on cheap, reliable oedometer tests with well-known closed-form solutions.

notes: S:e2827f7bd3f7 is flagged CONTESTED; it reports a past personal and scientific dispute, not disagreement among sources, so contested is false. History of soil mechanics rather than soil science: a candidate for the history part or for trimming.

title: Overburden pressure

definition.text: The pressure at a given depth caused by the weight of the overlying material, also called lithostatic pressure or vertical stress.

facts.text: It increases with depth in proportion to the density of the overlying material and gravity; in the Earth's crust the average gradient is about 270 bar/km.
It reduces porosity, shrinking volume without distorting the material, and so matters in diagenesis and metamorphism.
Horizontal stresses are hard to measure, so they are expressed through a lateral stress coefficient, k, relative to the vertical stress; Terzaghi in 1952 linked k to the rock's Poisson's ratio.
Together with excessive pore water pressure, overburden can force blocks out near the base of a river bank, a popout failure.

notes: The dossier's definition line (S:de6e66699c52) defines pressure in general; the definition uses the lead sentence S:afad8ef25824. Heim's rock-column theory left out as geodynamics.

title: Soil liquefaction

definition.text: The sudden loss of strength and stiffness in a saturated or partly saturated cohesionless soil under stress such as earthquake shaking, so that the solid behaves like a liquid.

facts.text: Loose sand tends to compress under load; if it is saturated, pore water pressure rises until it exceeds the contact forces between grains, and effective stress falls to essentially zero.
Dense sands tend instead to dilate, so loose, saturated, poorly drained sandy or non-plastic silty soils are the most likely to liquefy; gravels and clays rarely do.
The most susceptible deposits are young Holocene, well-sorted sands and silts in saturated beds metres thick, found along stream beds, beaches, dunes and areas of loess.
Allen Hazen first called soil 'liquefied' after the 1918 failure of the Calaveras Dam in California; engineers paid more attention after the 1964 Alaska and Niigata earthquakes.
Earthquake pressures can force water and liquefied sand to the surface as sand boils, and ground can slide sideways on slopes of only 1 or 2 degrees, called lateral spreading.
It damages buildings, bridges, buried services and levees; in the 2018 Palu earthquake it buried the suburb of Balaroa and Petobo village 3 metres deep in mud.
Over geological time, earthquake liquefaction may provide a dense parent material in which a fragipan can develop through pedogenesis.
Mitigation densifies soil by vibro or dynamic compaction or stabilises it with grout; microbially induced calcite precipitation has been proposed to cement liquefiable sand.

notes: Flow liquefaction, cyclic liquefaction and cyclic mobility (§ Technical definitions) left as geotechnical detail. The Quick clay and Turbidity currents sections are left to their own pages (Quick clay is an erosion-and-sediment seed).

title: Liquefaction potential analysis
article: Soil liquefaction#Liquefaction potential: simplified empirical analysis

definition.text: An engineering method that judges whether a soil will liquefy by comparing the earthquake load with the soil's capacity to resist liquefaction.

facts.text: It needs a field measure of resistance (standard or cone penetration resistance, or shear-wave velocity), the earthquake load as a cyclic stress ratio, and the soil's cyclic resistance ratio.
Building codes in many countries require engineers to consider liquefaction when designing buildings, bridges, embankment dams and retaining structures.

notes: Pure geotechnical design procedure, recorded only so the merge sees the decision; the process itself is the Soil liquefaction entry.

title: Quicksand

definition.text: A colloid of fine granular material, such as sand, silt or clay, and water that forms when saturated loose sand is agitated and loses its strength.

facts.text: It forms in standing water or where water flows upward, as from an artesian spring, so that the flow opposes gravity and suspends the grains.
It is a shear-thinning non-Newtonian fluid: undisturbed it looks solid, but a change in stress of less than 1% suddenly lowers its viscosity.
At about 2 grams per cubic centimetre it is roughly twice as dense as the human body, so a person cannot sink beyond about waist height.
Pulling a foot out at 1 cm/s takes as much force as lifting a car; slow leg movements and floating on the back allow escape.

notes: Soil liquefaction#Quicksand repeats the same material; Seepage#Pressures gives the zero-effective-stress view (S:9995d442c574).

title: Thixotropy

definition.text: A time-dependent shear-thinning property: a material that is thick at rest flows more easily when shaken or stressed, then takes time to thicken again.

facts.text: It arises because particles or structured solutes need time to organise; many gels and colloids are stable at rest but turn fluid when agitated.
Some clays are thixotropic, as are most bentonite suspensions, and slopes containing fuller's earth can become unstable when heavy rainfall saturates it.
Quick clay changes from a stiff solid to a liquid mass when disturbed, a change called spontaneous liquefaction or thixotropy; landslides such as the Aberfan disaster show the effect.
Herbert Freundlich coined the word, from the Greek for 'touch' and 'turn', for a sol–gel transformation.

notes: Most of the page covers paints, inks, foods and casting; only the clay and landslide sentences are drafted.

title: Soil matrix

definition.text: The solid phase of a soil: the mineral particles and organic matter that make it up.

facts.text: A soil is made of the solid matrix, a pore space holding the soil atmosphere, and a liquid phase, the soil solution, holding water and dissolved substances.
Matrix particles are classed by size and by mineralogy; texture largely sets properties such as hydraulic conductivity and water potential, but mineralogy can strongly modify them.
Gravel, sand and silt usually inherit their minerals from the parent material; quartz is the most common because it resists chemical weathering.
Clay, with its high specific surface area and unbalanced negative charges, is the most active mineral component, so its mineralogy matters most.
Clay minerals are secondary minerals, precipitates whose make-up differs from their parent materials, and they keep forming as long as the soil exists.
Humus is the organic component of the matrix; on a dry weight basis its cation exchange capacity is many times that of clay.
Nutrients held in exchangeable form on clay colloids and organic matter in the matrix are an accessible reservoir of plant nutrients such as K, Ca, Mg, P and Zn.
Water moving down through the matrix can carry fine clay from the upper to the lower part of a soil, the process called lessivage.

notes: The alumino-silica clay, organic colloid and terra preta sections are left to the chapters whose seeds they describe (Clay mineral, Humus, Terra preta, Biochar). Isomorphous substitution (Soil matrix, Soil, Montmorillonite) is left to the chemistry chapters.

title: Bearing capacity

definition.text: The capacity of soil to support loads applied to the ground, such as a foundation, without failing in shear.

facts.text: Ultimate bearing capacity is the theoretical maximum pressure before failure; the allowable value divides it by a factor of safety, or on soft soils is set by tolerable settlement.
It depends on the soil's shear strength and on the foundation's shape, size, depth and type; failure can be by general, local or punching shear.
Well-graded gravels have a large bearing capacity, about 8,000 pounds per square foot (39,000 kg/m2), with excellent drainage and low frost heave potential.
Soil structure affects traffic bearing capacity, along with root growth, water and gas movement and other soil functions.

notes: A foundation-engineering concept, kept because structure and compaction govern trafficability; Soil mechanics#Bearing capacity (chunk 03) may yield the same entry. The design formulas are the excluded entry Bearing capacity equations.

title: Bearing capacity equations

definition.text: Formulas for the ultimate bearing capacity of foundations, first set out comprehensively by Karl von Terzaghi for rough shallow foundations.

facts.text: Terzaghi's 1943 method for general shear failure accounts for soil cohesion, soil friction, embedment, surcharge and self-weight.
Meyerhof's 1951 theory extended the approach to rough shallow and deep foundations, adding shape, depth and inclination factors.

notes: Pure foundation-design procedure, recorded only so the merge sees the decision.

title: Seepage

definition.text: The movement of water through soil.

facts.text: Where pore water pressure rises evenly with depth below the water table, conditions are hydrostatic and water does not flow; a sloping or perched water table makes it seep.
Under Darcy's law, flow through a porous medium is proportional to the rate of change of excess pressure with distance, scaled by the soil's permeability and the fluid's viscosity.
Hydraulic conductivity varies by many orders of magnitude with soil type, from about 10−12 m/s in clays to about 10−1 m/s in gravels.
In steady seepage velocities do not change with time; that does not hold while water tables are changing or the soil is consolidating.
Upward seepage reduces effective stress; at the critical hydraulic gradient it reaches zero, the soil loses nearly all strength, and less permeable layers may heave.
This zero-effective-stress state is also called liquefaction, quicksand or a boiling condition, and strength loss from upward seepage often contributes to levee failures.
Fast seepage drags soil particles away from its exit point and the erosion works back upgradient as soil piping, which can fail a structure and form sinkholes.
Bentonite, a clay almost fully saturated with sodium, is used to build impermeable curtains in the ground, for example below dams, to stop seepage.

notes: Soil mechanics#Seepage: steady state flow of water (chunk 03) may yield the same entry. Piping is named in related as Internal erosion (an erosion-and-sediment page).

title: Flow nets

definition.text: A traditional graphical method for two-dimensional seepage problems, drawing flow lines along the direction of flow and equipotential lines of constant total head.

facts.text: In two or three dimensions steady seepage obeys Laplace's equation, which computer programs now solve.

notes: Pure engineering calculation procedure, recorded only so the merge sees the decision.

definition.text: A spot where water under pressure wells up through a bed of sand or mud, looking as if it were boiling.

facts.text: Ejected sand can build a cone, a sand volcano or sand blow, with slopes at the sand's angle of repose and a crater at the top, from millimetres to metres across.
Earthquakes that liquefy saturated sediment produce them; the 1811–1812 New Madrid earthquakes left the largest known, 'The Beach' near Hayti, Missouri, 2.3 kilometres long.
In floods, hydraulic head pushes water through a levee; turbulent flow at the seep starts soil piping, which can quickly fail the embankment, so sandbag rings are stacked to slow it.
Liquefaction features such as sand blows and clastic dikes are mapped as strong evidence of past earthquakes.

title: Specific storage and storativity

definition.text: The volume of water that a unit volume of saturated aquifer releases from storage when the hydraulic head falls by one unit.

facts.text: Storativity, or the storage coefficient, is the dimensionless volume released per unit area of aquifer per unit fall in head; for a confined aquifer it is specific storage summed over thickness.
Specific storage reflects the compressibility of both the aquifer and the water itself.
In an unconfined aquifer storativity roughly equals the specific yield, because release from specific storage is orders of magnitude smaller.
Laboratory consolidation tests give the coefficient of consolidation and vertical hydraulic conductivity, whose ratio yields the inelastic skeletal specific storage used in land-subsidence models.

notes: Hydrogeology page assigned to this chapter by the graph; marginal for a soil course.

definition.text: The fraction of a material's bulk volume that drains out under gravity, also called drainable porosity.

facts.text: Average specific yield is 2% for clay, 8% for silt, 21% for fine sand and 27% for coarse sand.
Dune sand yields about 38% and loess about 18%, while till that is mostly silt yields only about 6%.
It is used mainly for unconfined aquifers, where the elastic storage from specific storage is small by comparison.

definition.text: A material's weight per unit volume, also called unit weight, equal to its density multiplied by gravitational acceleration.

facts.text: Its SI unit is the newton per cubic metre; water at 4 °C weighs 9.807 kilonewtons per cubic metre.
Unlike density it is not a fixed property of a material, because gravitational acceleration varies with location.
Soil mechanics uses it for earthwork problems, distinguishing moist, dry and saturated unit weight by whether the pores hold water and air, air only, or water only.
Each is calculated from the specific gravity of the solids, the void ratio and the unit weight of water, with the water content for moist soil.

definition.text: The change in volume of a granular material when it is sheared; dense packings expand rather than compress.

facts.text: Osborne Reynolds first described it scientifically in 1885/1886, and Peter Walter Rowe brought it into geotechnical engineering.
Grains in a dense packing interlock and cannot slip past one another, so shearing levers them apart and the bulk expands; a very loose material compacts instead.
On a wet beach the sand around a walker's foot seems to dry, because the foot expands the sand and water moves into the new space between grains.
The denser the soil, the more it expands; its friction angle peaks and then drops abruptly, so slopes, footings, tunnels and piles in such soils must allow for the loss.

definition.text: The sinking of land caused by unsustainable pumping of groundwater.

facts.text: Aquifers often include compressible silt or clay layers; pumping changes the effective stress and causes consolidation, often irreversible, which reduces their volume and lowers the surface.
One estimate ties 80% of serious U.S. land subsidence problems to excessive groundwater extraction; there the land sank 1 m for every 13 m that the water table was lowered.
Generations of pumping for crops have made the whole San Joaquin Valley sink, and areas such as New Orleans now face severe flooding from subsidence.
Permanent compaction of fine layers can destroy much of an aquifer's storage; in Arizona the land kept subsiding for decades after water levels recovered by 100 ft.

title: Lateral earth pressure

definition.text: The pressure that soil exerts in the horizontal direction.

facts.text: Its coefficient, K, is the ratio of horizontal to vertical effective stress; the in situ earth pressure at rest is the overburden stress times K0.
It affects the consolidation and strength of soil and is used to design retaining walls, basements, tunnels, deep foundations and braced excavations.
Coulomb first studied it in 1776, Rankine's 1857 theory predicts active and passive pressures, and Bell extended Rankine's theory to soils with cohesion as well as friction.

notes: Geotechnical design concept for retaining structures, beyond what a soil science course needs. Its many coefficient theories (Coulomb, Rankine, Caquot–Kerisel, Mononobe–Okabe, Pantelidis) were not drafted. Soil mechanics#Lateral earth pressure (chunk 03) may yield the same entry.

title: Terzaghi's principle

definition.text: The principle that a load on a porous material such as soil is opposed partly by the fluid pressure in its pores, so that its measurable responses follow changes in effective stress.

facts.text: Karl von Terzaghi introduced it in a series of papers in the 1920s, from studying how buildings consolidated the soil beneath them.
Effective stress is total stress minus pore pressure, because the pore fluid bears part of the load and partly unloads the solid matrix.

It suits soil because its silica grains are effectively incompressible, so volume changes come from grains rearranging; Maurice Biot generalised it to compressible solids in the 1940s, founding poroelasticity.
Experiments contradict some assumptions: Darcy's law fails at high gradients, permeability and compressibility fall during consolidation, and the void ratio–effective stress relation depends on time.

notes: Close to Effective stress (chunk 04 seed); merge into that entry if it already states the principle.

definition.text: A device that tests the strength of a material, such as soil, by measuring how far a probe sinks into it.

facts.text: Soil penetrometers, usually round or cone-shaped, are dropped on or pressed into the soil and the depth of the hole is measured, showing for example whether the ground is strong enough to carry a road.
On farmland, the rise in soil strength caused by compaction can be measured with a penetrometer.
The fall cone test, also called the cone penetrometer test, measures a soil's liquid limit, and its results do not depend on the operator's skill or judgement.
Penetrometers also gauge soil moisture, including on space probes such as Huygens on Titan, and test glacier beds, cricket pitches and, since 2009, British racecourses.

definition.text: The branch of civil engineering concerned with the engineering behaviour of earth materials.

facts.text: It applies soil mechanics and rock mechanics, drawing also on geology, hydrology and geophysics.
It overlaps with engineering geology, but geotechnical engineering is a specialty of civil engineering and engineering geology a specialty of geology.
Until the 18th century soil design had no theoretical basis and relied on experience; problems such as the Leaning Tower of Pisa pushed engineers toward science.
In 1773 Charles Coulomb applied mechanics to earth pressures on ramparts, taking shear strength on a slip plane as cohesion plus friction.
Nineteenth-century foundations included Darcy's law of flow through porous media, Atterberg's clay consistency indices and Reynolds's 1885 finding that shearing dilates dense granular material.
Modern geotechnics is dated to Karl von Terzaghi's Erdbaumechanik of 1925; he showed that effective stress controls soil shear strength and framed bearing-capacity and consolidation theory.
In 1958 Roscoe, Schofield and Wroth linked volume change and shearing through critical state soil mechanics, the basis of many advanced soil models.
In foundation design the main concerns are bearing capacity, settlement and ground movement beneath the foundation.

definition.text: Site exploration that gathers the physical properties of the soil and rock under and beside a site, to design earthworks and foundations.

facts.text: It combines surface and subsurface exploration, sampling and laboratory testing, sometimes with geophysics such as seismic, resistivity and ground-penetrating radar surveys.
Subsurface work usually includes in-situ tests such as the standard and cone penetration tests, and may use test pits and trenches.
The standard penetration test's split-spoon sampler collects disturbed samples; thin-walled piston samplers collect less disturbed ones.
Centrifuge models reach prototype-scale stresses in small models, which matters because soil strength and stiffness depend on confining pressure.

definition.text: A mathematical model of how materials fail under combined shear and normal stress, used to define the shear strength of soils and rocks at different effective stresses.

facts.text: Its failure criterion is the straight-line envelope τ = σ tan(ϕ) + c, where c is the cohesion and ϕ the angle of internal friction.
It is named for Charles-Augustin de Coulomb, who wrote a 1776 essay on it, and Christian Otto Mohr, who generalised it near the end of the 19th century.
Coulomb's friction hypothesis gives the stress combination that causes failure; Mohr's circle gives the principal stresses that produce it and the angle of the failure plane.
It generally applies to materials whose compressive strength far exceeds their tensile strength.
With ϕ = 0 it reduces to the Tresca criterion; in three dimensions its failure surface is a cone with a hexagonal cross-section.
Cohesion cannot be determined precisely because it is not a fundamental soil property, yet the theory is still used in practice.
It omits the dilation many geomaterials show under triaxial stress, so plasticity models often pair it with a smooth non-associated flow potential.
Typical friction angles are 30° to 45° for sand, 35° for gravel and 26° to 35° for silt; clay cohesion is 10 to 200 kPa.

definition.text: A laboratory test that measures a soil's consolidation properties by loading a sample and recording how it deforms.

facts.text: It reproduces the one-dimensional deformation and drainage soils undergo in the field, to predict how they deform when effective stress changes.
A disc of soil about three times as wide as it is high sits in a rigid ring that stops sideways movement, between porous stones that let water drain.
Saturated samples consolidate gradually over minutes or hours; thickness against time gives the coefficient of consolidation and the soil's permeability.

In the common incremental loading test each load stays until primary consolidation ends before the next is added; a load increment ratio of 1/2 gives enough points to relate void ratio to effective stress.
It yields the preconsolidation pressure, the effective stress dividing stiff from soft response, which usually reflects past loading by glaciers or eroded layers.
It also yields the compression index Cc = Δe/Δlogσ'v for loads above the preconsolidation pressure, the recompression index below it, and the secondary compression index Cα = Δe/Δlog t.

Frontard ran the first consolidation experiments in 1910; Terzaghi began his in 1919 and published his consolidation theory in 1923, and Casagrande devised a method to estimate preconsolidation pressure.
Standard procedures include ASTM D2435, BS 1377-5:1990 and ISO 17892-5:2017.

definition.text: The porosity, pore sizes, pore-size distribution and pore shapes, roughness and tortuosity that together describe the pores of a porous medium.

facts.text: Pore structure and fluid flow are closely linked: it controls intrinsic permeability and affects hydraulic conductivity and the capacity to retain fluids.
Pore space is usefully pictured as a network of channels, with wide pore bodies joined by narrow pore throats or necks.
Pore size, usually the effective radius of a pore body or neck, arguably has the broadest effect of any pore property.
A soil's pore-size distribution, a function f(r) of effective radius, gives the relative abundance of each pore size and has textural and structural parts.
In soils pore size does not simply follow particle size: clays promote aggregation and so large pores between aggregates.
Subdividing the pore-size distribution can express complex soil behaviour such as the hysteresis of soil water retention.
Mercury intrusion porosimetry and gas adsorption measure pore-size distribution; mercury needs 140 MPa to enter pores smaller than 10 nm.
Pore morphology covers the shape, surface roughness and tortuosity of the pore channels holding liquid and gas.

definition.text: A material containing pores, with a solid skeleton called the matrix and pores usually filled with a liquid or gas.

facts.text: Rocks and soils, for example aquifers, are porous media, and the concept is used in soil mechanics and hydrogeology.
It is mostly characterised by porosity; permeability, strength, conductivity and tortuosity can sometimes be derived from the constituents and pore structure, but not simply.
Solid matrix and pore network are often both continuous, like a sponge; effective porosity is the pore space open to flow.
Darcy's law describes flow through fine-porous media, Forchheimer's law flow through coarse ones.

definition.text: The smallest volume over which a measurement gives a value representative of the whole material.

facts.text: Measurements on porous samples that are too small oscillate; as the sample grows they settle, and the size at which they become consistent is the REV.
Readings stay stable with larger samples until other hydrostratigraphic layers are included, a size called the maximum elementary volume.
The groundwater flow equation has to be defined in an REV.
An REV assumes a heterogeneous material can be replaced by an equivalent homogeneous one, but its size varies with the property studied.

definition.text: The ratio of a path's actual length to the straight-line distance between its ends, used to predict transport through porous media such as soils.

facts.text: Hydraulic, electrical, diffusional and thermal tortuosities describe different transport processes, and geometrical tortuosity describes pore shape; the concept has many definitions.
The simplest measure is the arc-chord ratio, which equals 1 for a straight line.
In hydrogeology it is the ratio of diffusivity in free space to diffusivity in the porous medium; strictly, effective diffusivity varies with the inverse square of geometrical tortuosity.
In soils, flow-path tortuosity controls diffusion during leaching, and the tortuosity of macropores indicates their resistance to water flow.

definition.text: Repeated walking on the ground by humans or animals.

facts.text: Trampling destroys the above-ground parts of many plants and compacts the soil, creating a distinct microenvironment.
Recreational trampling in alpine areas raises bulk density and lowers porosity, altering soil moisture and temperature and increasing runoff and erosion.
Plots trampled in the Belianske Tatras in 2008 and retested in 2022 showed that apparent recovery can hide species losses, so impacts may be delayed.
Grazing animals can also aerate soil by trampling, and planned herd trampling is credited with aiding infiltration and soil carbon storage.

title: Soil strength

definition.text: The resistance a soil offers to deformation, measured in the field as its resistance to a penetrometer.

facts.text: It comes mainly from friction between particles, which is proportional to normal stress, so pore water pressure, by lowering normal stress, weakens soil.
A small amount of water bridging the gaps between grains increases it through attraction to mineral surfaces.
High strength in drying soils, as in hardsetting soils, restricts seedling and root growth; it is one of the limits that define the non-limiting water range.
Bonding grains with microbially induced calcite and making the soil denser both raise its strength.

notes: Phrase concept with no page of its own; used on many in-scope pages (Effective stress, Soil compaction (agriculture), Soil structure, Nonlimiting water range, Angle of repose).
